overview: Systems keep arriving from the Pacific through the week. A weak one brings light snow Sunday, a break Monday, then a stronger storm by Tuesday that hits the Cascades and Sierra hardest. Coast Mountains get a wetter mix with rain mixing in by midweek.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A weak system brings light snow to mountains from Saturday into Sunday, with little impact expected. A break follows Monday, then a front arrives Tuesday, with snow levels near 2,500 feet early. Mt. Baker and Crystal Mountain each get most of their totals Tuesday, with 15 inches apiece for the week. Rain and snow mix by Wednesday.

regions.title: Tahoe
regions.text: A weak system brings light snow Sunday and a dry Monday. A stronger storm arrives midweek and brings snow to the Sierra, though forecasters expect less than the last storm. Sugar Bowl sees the highest totals, with 13 inches. The NWS is calling for more, 11 to 21 inches from Sunday through Wednesday night at Sugar Bowl. Expect cold valley fog Saturday morning.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Snow mostly stays light through Monday at Whistler and Cypress. Wetter weather moves in Tuesday as rain mixes in, and by Wednesday the snow level rises and rain dominates. Whistler gets its biggest day Tuesday, at 7 inches, for 15 inches in total.

regions.title: Eastern Sierra
regions.text: Expect cold, clear nights with valley fog Saturday. A fast, weak system brings light snow Sunday, with a bigger storm midweek that could make travel difficult. Forecasters suggest the best travel window is Monday afternoon through Tuesday evening. Mammoth's biggest day is Sunday, with 5 inches.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
